summary: A survey of which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP, this edition run in February 1983. It continues a series by David Smallberg. Replaced by RFC 843.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on every computer's door to see which would answer. This is one week's tally.

subtitle: A February 1983 survey of TCP support on Internet hosts, continuing the tracking of rapid TCP adoption.

tldr.problem: As TCP adoption accelerated, maintaining current knowledge of which hosts supported TCP became increasingly valuable for network operators planning services.
tldr.mechanism: Smallberg tested 328 hosts (an increase from the 323 previously tested) in February 1983, using the same methodology to test Telnet, FTP, and SMTP support and tracking which hosts had come online or gone offline.
tldr.outcome: Results show significant growth: 183 hosts accepted Telnet, 170 accepted FTP, and 169 accepted SMTP. Some hosts that were dead in January were now active, and new hosts had been added to the test list, reflecting the rapidly growing Internet.

today: RFC 842 was superseded by RFC 843 in 1983. Like the earlier surveys in this series, it provides a valuable historical record of the rapid growth and adoption of TCP during the critical formative years of the Internet, before the explosion of the World Wide Web in the 1990s.

sections.title: The February Survey
sections.content:
RFC 842 continues the survey series with tests run in February 1983, about a month after RFC 839. By February, the test scope had expanded to 328 hosts (up from 323), reflecting the rapid growth of the network. The tests were conducted from 1 February to 3 February, with primary testing on 1 and 2 February and retests of unreachable and dead hosts on 3 February.

The growing list of hosts reflects the explosive expansion of the Internet during the early 1980s, when new institutions were connecting almost weekly.
sections.eli5: A month later, the same person tested even more computers. The list had grown larger because the Internet was expanding fast.

sections.title: Test Scope and Methods
sections.content:
This survey tested 328 hosts from the NIC hostname table as of 28 January 1983. The core testing ran on 1 February from 10 am to 1 pm PST, continuing on 2 February from 8 am to 11:15 am PST, with additional retesting on 3 February morning.

The test host base expanded from the previous surveys, but the testing methodology remained consistent. This allowed comparison with earlier surveys while also tracking the growth of the network. All three services (Telnet, FTP, and SMTP) were tested on every host.
sections.eli5: The testing used the same method as before, but now there were more computers to test. The test spread across two days because there were so many hosts.

sections.title: Results from February 1983
sections.content:
183 hosts accepted Telnet connections out of 214 claiming support, 170 accepted FTP out of 198 claiming it, and 169 accepted SMTP out of 176 claiming it. The dead host count was 65, down from 53 in January, suggesting that some infrastructure problems were being resolved even as the network added new machines.

The February results show robust growth in actual TCP support. The acceptance rates for all three services had climbed since January, with Telnet reaching 161 accepting out of 214 claiming support. The data demonstrates that not only was the network growing in size, but also in reliability and TCP adoption.
sections.eli5: More computers were talking to each other. Telnet hit 161, FTP 150, and SMTP 134. Dead computers fell to 65, which is better than before.

sections.title: What This Shows About Growth
sections.content:
By February 1983, the TCP/IP suite had become the de facto standard for network communication on the Internet. The surveys show a clear progression: from 172 hosts accepting Telnet in mid-January to 182 in late January to 161 claiming and receiving Telnet in February. The expansion from 323 to 328 hosts tested seems small, but it represents new institutions joining the network.

These surveys capture a pivotal moment when TCP was transitioning from an experimental protocol to the backbone of Internet communication. The growth in both the number of connected hosts and the reliability of TCP services demonstrates rapid institutional adoption and deployment across universities, government agencies, and research centers.
sections.eli5: By now, it was clear that TCP was winning. Almost all computers that claimed to support it actually did. The Internet was growing from a research project into a network that mattered.
